title: YouTube / Video Streaming
subtitle: Video streaming platform: resumable chunked uploads, DAG transcoding, ABR packaging, and edge CDN delivery.
keyTakeaways: Never process raw multi-gigabyte video uploads as a single monolithic file: use S3 presigned multipart uploads and split video files at Group-of-Pictures (GOP) keyframe boundaries so worker clusters can transcode 4-second chunks in parallel.

Deliver smooth playback over fluctuating cellular networks using Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) streaming (HLS / DASH): client players measure buffer health and network throughput to switch dynamically between 360p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K at chunk boundaries.

Apply multi-tier CDN storage: cache the top 5% viral videos on edge NVMe SSDs near users, keep the next 20% in regional origin shields, and store long-tail archival videos in cold cloud object storage.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A global Video Streaming Platform allows creators to upload high-definition video files, transcodes them into multiple resolutions, and streams them reliably to millions of concurrent viewers worldwide.
bullets: Functional: Resumable chunked video upload; asynchronous transcoding into multiple resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K); Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) streaming playback.
Functional: Video metadata management (title, description, tags, view count) and thumbnail extraction.
Non-Functional: Sub-2 second video startup latency; minimal buffering during playback over fluctuating mobile connections.
Non-Functional: High durability for uploaded master videos (99.999999999% via cloud object storage).
Out of Scope: Live streaming real-time WebRTC ingest, automated copyrighted content fingerprint matching, and real-time ad insertion auctions.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Video platforms have massive storage and egress bandwidth demands driven by asymmetric upload vs view ratios.
bullets: Upload Volume: 500 hours of video uploaded every minute (~30,000 hours/hour, or ~720,000 hours/day).
Viewer Volume: 1 billion daily active views averaging 10 minutes of watch time = 10 billion minutes of video streamed/day.
Storage Ingestion: Average raw upload bitrate = 20 Mbps (~9 GB/hour). Daily master storage ingest = 720,000 * 9 GB = ~6.48 PB/day.
Transcoded Storage: Transcoding into 4 resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) adds ~4x storage overhead, requiring ~25 PB of new storage daily.
Egress Bandwidth: 10 billion minutes/day at average 3 Mbps streaming bitrate = ~3.75 Tbps of continuous outbound CDN bandwidth.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Bandwidth and storage calculations demonstrate why video platforms rely completely on distributed edge CDNs and chunk-level transcoding pipelines.
bullets: Egress bandwidth scale: 10 billion minutes / 86,400 seconds = ~115,000 concurrent streaming hours per second. At 3 Mbps average bitrate = ~345 Gbps baseline, peaking at 1.5 to 2 Tbps during peak evening hours.
CDN offload requirement: No origin data center can afford 2 Tbps of direct egress. The edge CDN must achieve a 95%+ Cache Hit Ratio (CHR) to keep origin traffic under 100 Gbps.
Transcoding compute sizing: Transcoding 720,000 hours of video daily within 24 hours requires a distributed fleet capable of processing 30,000 hours of video per hour in parallel.

codeSnippet.title: YouTube Video Streaming Capacity & Storage Estimation Sheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT (QPS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Uploads per Day (5-min avg)            : 8,640,000 videos/day (500 hrs/min)
Upload Init QPS (Avg / Peak 2.5x)      : 100 QPS / 250 QPS
Upload Chunk PUT QPS (8MB chunks)      : ~7,000 chunk PUTs/sec avg

Daily Video Views                      : 5,000,000,000 views/day
Playback Manifest Start QPS (Avg/Peak) : 57,870 QPS / 144,675 QPS
4-Sec Segment Fetch QPS (CDN Edge)     : (5B * 90 segs) / 86,400 = 5,208,333 QPS
Peak CDN Segment Fetch QPS (2.5x)      : 13,020,833 QPS

================================================================================
2. METADATA & VIEW COUNTER MEMORY (REDIS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Hot Video Metadata Cache (100M videos) : 100,000,000 * 1 KB = 100 GB RAM
Write-Behind Sharded View Counters     : 20M active videos * 256 B = 5.12 GB RAM
Total Redis Cluster Footprint          : ~128 GB per geographic region

================================================================================
3. 5-YEAR VIDEO STORAGE (MULTI-RESOLUTION ABR LADDER)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
New Video Minutes Uploaded / Day       : 720,000 hrs * 60 = 43,200,000 mins/day
Storage per Minute (240p..4K + Audio)  : ~187.5 MB / minute
Daily Transcoded Video Storage         : 43.2M * 187.5 MB = 8.10 PB / day
5-Year Raw Video Storage               : 8.10 PB * 365 * 5 = 14.78 Exabytes (EB)
With Reed-Solomon (10+4) Erasure Coding: 14.78 EB * 1.4 = 20.69 EB
  (Note: Cold videos with 0 views in 180 days discard intermediate VP9/AV1
   renditions and retain only H.264 + source, cutting cold storage by 60%!)

================================================================================
4. GLOBAL NETWORK BANDWIDTH
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Upload Ingress (30,000 video-sec/s)    : 30,000 * 1.875 MB/s = 56.25 GB/s (450 Gbps)
Concurrent Active Viewers (Avg)        : (5B * 360s) / 86,400s = 20,833,333 viewers
Streaming Egress (Avg @ 3.5 Mbps)      : 20.83M * 3.5 Mbps = 72.9 Tbps (9.11 TB/s)
Streaming Egress (Peak 2.5x)           : 182.3 Tbps (96% offloaded at ISP CDN Edge)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Video APIs must support multipart resumable upload sessions, manifest retrieval, and metadata queries.
bullets: Upload Initiation: `POST /v1/videos/upload-session` returns `{ uploadId, presignedChunkUrls: [...] }`.
Playback API: `GET /v1/videos/{videoId}/master.m3u8` returns the HLS master playlist referencing sub-playlists for 360p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K.
Metadata Schema (PostgreSQL/CockroachDB): Stores `video_id`, `uploader_id`, `title`, `duration`, `status` (`UPLOADING`, `TRANSCODING`, `READY`), and manifest URLs.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The video architecture separates the ingestion and transcoding pipeline from the streaming CDN delivery path.
bullets: Upload Service: Generates S3 presigned multipart URLs so client mobile devices upload chunks directly to S3 buckets, bypassing application servers.
Transcoding Orchestrator (DAG Pipeline): Triggers on S3 upload completion, splits raw video into 4-second GOP chunks, and schedules parallel FFmpeg tasks.
Transcoding Worker Fleet: Spot/Preemptible GPU instances running containerized FFmpeg workers that output fragmented MP4 (fMP4) chunks.
Storage Tier: Cloud object storage (S3) holding master videos, video segments, and `.m3u8` playlist files.
Global CDN Tier: Edge POPs that cache 4-second video segments close to viewers worldwide.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Transcoding multi-gigabyte videos sequentially takes hours. Splitting videos into independent keyframe chunks enables near-real-time parallel processing.
bullets: GOP (Group of Pictures) chunking: A video consists of keyframes (I-frames) followed by delta frames (P/B-frames). Split the master file strictly at I-frame boundaries into 4-second segments so each chunk can be decoded and encoded independently.

Parallel DAG transcoding: A 60-minute video yields 900 chunks. Distribute the 900 chunks across 100 worker containers. All chunks transcode in parallel within 2 to 3 minutes, followed by a stitcher step that writes the master HLS manifest.

Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) switching: The client video player monitors download speed and buffer fullness. If buffer health drops below 4 seconds, the player switches to downloading the 720p chunk instead of 1080p, preventing playback stalls.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Optimizing CDN cache efficiency and handling spot instance interruptions are central to video platform economics.
bullets: Spot instance termination handling: Transcoding workers run on cheap cloud Spot/Preemptible instances. Because chunks are small (4 seconds), if a spot instance is reclaimed, the orchestrator simply reschedules that single chunk on another worker.

Pre-warming video manifests: When a video from a popular creator goes live, push the master playlist and first three 4-second chunks to regional CDN edge caches before notifying subscribers, eliminating the initial stampede on origin storage.
Tiered storage lifecycle: After 30 days, move master raw upload files to cold archival storage (Glacier), keeping only optimized ABR chunks on standard object storage.

tradeOffs.pros: Massive parallelization; a 2-hour 4K video transcodes in minutes; spot instance reclaims only drop a 4-second task.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires complex DAG orchestration and precise I-frame boundary splitting logic.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large-scale video platforms (YouTube, Netflix, Vimeo) processing thousands of hours daily.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple architecture; run FFmpeg directly on a single large compute instance.
tradeOffs.cons: Takes hours for long videos; if the instance crashes at 98%, the entire transcoding job must restart from scratch.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small internal video tools or low-traffic platforms with short (< 2 minute) video clips.

tradeOffs.option: Direct S3 Presigned Uploads vs Gateway Proxying
tradeOffs.pros: Client uploads go directly to object storage; zero upload bandwidth or memory overhead on application servers.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires client-side multipart chunk management and S3 webhook integration for upload completion.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Any production platform handling user-generated video or large file uploads.

interviewTip: Never propose uploading or transcoding a 10 GB video file as a single monolithic unit. Explain how S3 presigned multipart uploads handle the upload, and how splitting the video at GOP (Group of Pictures) boundaries allows hundreds of worker containers to transcode chunks in parallel.
